newsitem.title: PERU: Yanacocha keeps Peru's Buenaventura's Q3 in black.
newsitem.headline: Yanacocha keeps Peru's Buenaventura's Q3 in black.

text.p: Buenaventura's minority stake in South America's largest gold mine, Yanacocha, saved the Peruvian mining company from a third quarter net loss despite rising costs due to its promising but expensive exploration program, analysts and company officials said.

The company's ambitious exploration projects should mean Buenaventura will sooner or later add new profitable assets to its portfolio and outweigh the current losses in its four wholly-owned, but small, operating mines, they added.

Buenaventura's third quarter net income fell slightly to 14.8 million soles from 15.2 million soles in the same period last year, but notably the company also saw an operating loss of 4.5 million soles, compared to operating income of 5.8 million soles last year.

The "extremely successful" Minera Yanacocha S.A., a joint venture run by Newmont Mining Co in the northern Peruvian Andes, is "clearly Buenaventura's principal asset", according to the firm's financial manager Carlos Galvez.
Yanacocha produced in the third quarter 219,400 ounces of gold, more than 50 percent higher than the previous year.

This allowed the polymetallic miner to record "related earnings" of 19.9 million soles from Yanacocha and "keep Buenaventura in the black for the third quarter," said Josilu Carbonel, mining analyst at Santander Investment in Lima.

The Yanacocha gains would have been even better if it were not for a legal dispute that forces the miner to base these earnings on a a 32.3 percent stake, instead of the 43.65 share that analysts are confident will be the eventual outcome of the litigation.

In part, Buenaventura's operating loss was due to reduced sales income - 52.9 million soles compared to 66.7 million soles - caused by lower silver prices and two delayed concentrate shipments worth 11.0 million soles.

But the main reason for the operating loss is the company's bet for the future on its exploration projects - a strategy "acceptable to the market because of the company's sound fundamentals," according to Carbonel.

With an exploration budget of $8 million this year and $11.5 million for 1997, Buenaventura has a policy of running high operating costs, conscious of the strong potential of turning up reserves that could convert into profit-making mines.
"At the moment, all the effort going into Buenaventura's exploration plan, is being carried in cost terms by our small operations," said Galvez.
"This will be the case until one of our exploration projects turns into a new operating asset."
Carbonel agreed that with no immediate plans for Yanacocha to increase its current production levels, "the succcess of its expensive exploration program is what will determine Buenaventura's growth."
And the company's investment seems money well spent.
Buenaventura has two other projects in the same Cajamarca region as Yanacocha, which could rival the region's largest mine.

At both Minas Conga, another Newmont-Buenaventura joint venture, and at Tanta Huatay, where Buenaventura partners Southern Peru Copper Corp, the deposits could end up equalling Yanacocha in size, according to analysts.

Furthermore, Buenaventura's 100 percent-owned Caolin prospect - just to the south of Peru's hottest gold project Pierina, acquired in August by Barrick Gold Corp for $1 billion from Arequipa Resources Ltd - also has "very good potential," Carbonel said.
To cut its current operating losses, Buenaventura is also working to simplify the structure of the company and reduce costs at its "most important" wholly-owned mine, Uchucchacua, Galvez said.
Buenaventura's decision to absorb the companies operating two of these mines - Compania Orcopampa S.A. and Compania de Minas Recuperadas S.A. - was "welcome" to investors, Carbonel said.

And while Orcopampa is profitable but small, Recuperada is largely an exploration project and a third company mine, Julcani, is "old, difficult and expensive," it is at Uchucchacua where Buenaventura plans to invest, Galvez said.

The $4 million construction of a power line connecting Uchucchacua to the national electricity grid, scheduled for the first quarter of next year, will cut the mine's total operating costs by 15 percent, Galvez said.
-- Lima newsroom, 511 221-2134
